draft.title: Style
card: Style is the distinctive way a text is written. It is how something is said, not only what is said.

Style is built from four parts: vocabulary (the words chosen), sentence patterns (short or long, simple or complex), imagery (pictures made in the mind) and form (how the text is laid out, such as a poem, a letter or a script).
Style can belong to a writer, a time period, a culture or a genre. A genre is a type of text, such as mystery or fantasy, with familiar features.
Two texts can tell the same event in different styles. One might use short, blunt sentences and plain words. Another might use long, flowing sentences and rich imagery.
draft.remember: Style is how a text is written: its words, sentences, imagery and form.

a.q: Which of these best describes a text's style?
opts: The distinctive way it is written, not just what it says
The main message the writer wants readers to take away
The place and time in which the story is set
The order in which the events of the story happen
a.why: Style is about how a text is written, including its vocabulary, sentence patterns, imagery and form. The message is a different idea. It is the tempting wrong option, because style is about how something is said, not what the writer wants to say.
a.clue: Think of how something is said, not what is said.

b.q: Two students write about a storm. Sam uses short, blunt sentences and plain words. Lina uses long, flowing sentences and imagery of beasts and thunder. What is the main difference between their texts?
b.why: Both write about a storm, so the topic is the same. They differ in sentence patterns, vocabulary and imagery, which are the parts of style. Topic is the tempting wrong option, but it is what is written about, not how it is written.
b.clue: Both texts are about the same thing. What has changed is how it is written.

a.best: The distinctive way it is written, not just what it says
